question.text: The average of four numbers is 20. When one number is removed the average of the remaining three is 22. The number removed is:
question.explanation: Original sum = 80 and the remaining sum = 66, so the number removed is 80 - 66 = 14.

question.text: The average age of 30 students is 14 years. When the teacher's age is included the average becomes 15 years. The teacher's age is:
question.explanation: Total of 31 people = 31 x 15 = 465 years and the students total 30 x 14 = 420, so the teacher is 45.

question.text: The average of the first five multiples of 3 is:
question.explanation: The multiples are 3, 6, 9, 12 and 15; their sum 45 divided by 5 gives 9.

question.text: The average of all even numbers from 2 to 20 inclusive is:

question.text: The mean of six numbers is 15. If every number is multiplied by 3, the new mean is:

question.text: The average marks of 40 students is 62. If 25 of them average 68, the average of the remaining 15 students is:

question.text: The average of five consecutive odd numbers is 27. The largest of them is:
question.explanation: The middle number is 27, so the numbers are 23, 25, 27, 29 and 31, the largest being 31.

question.text: A can do a piece of work in 10 days and B in 15 days. Working together they will finish it in:
question.explanation: Combined one-day work = 1/10 + 1/15 = 1/6, so together they take 6 days.

question.text: A completes a job in 12 days and B completes the same job in 24 days. Working together they will complete it in:
question.explanation: Combined one-day work = 1/12 + 1/24 = 3/24 = 1/8, so they take 8 days.

question.text: If 15 men can complete a work in 20 days, then 25 men will complete it in:
question.explanation: Total work = 15 x 20 = 300 man-days, so 25 men need 300/25 = 12 days.

question.text: A can do a work in 20 days. He works for 5 days and leaves, and B, who alone can do the whole work in 30 days, finishes the remainder in:
question.explanation: A completes 5/20 = 1/4 of the work, so B must do 3/4 of it, taking 3/4 x 30 = 22.5 days.

question.text: A and B together finish a work in 12 days while A alone finishes it in 20 days. B alone will take:
question.explanation: B's one-day work = 1/12 - 1/20 = 5/60 - 3/60 = 2/60 = 1/30, so B alone takes 30 days.

question.text: One pipe fills a tank in 6 hours and another fills it in 12 hours. Opened together they will fill it in:
question.explanation: Combined rate = 1/6 + 1/12 = 3/12 = 1/4 of the tank per hour, so 4 hours are needed.

question.text: Pipe A fills a tank in 10 hours while pipe B empties the full tank in 15 hours. With both pipes open the tank fills in:
question.explanation: Net filling rate = 1/10 - 1/15 = 3/30 - 2/30 = 1/30 per hour, so the tank fills in 30 hours.

question.text: A is twice as good a workman as B and together they finish a work in 12 days. B alone will finish it in:
question.explanation: Their rates are in the ratio 2 : 1, so B does one-third of the joint work and needs 3 x 12 = 36 days.

Twelve men working 6 hours a day complete a job in 10 days. Fifteen men working 8 hours a day will complete the same job in:

question.text: A and B together complete a work in 8 days, while A, B and C together complete it in 6 days. C alone will complete it in:
question.explanation: C's one-day work = 1/6 - 1/8 = 4/24 - 3/24 = 1/24, so C alone takes 24 days.

question.text: If 5 machines produce 500 units in 10 hours, the number of units 8 identical machines will produce in the same 10 hours is:
question.explanation: Each machine makes 100 units in 10 hours, so 8 machines make 8 x 100 = 800 units.

question.text: A car covers 240 km in 4 hours. Its average speed is:
question.explanation: Speed = distance/time = 240/4 = 60 km/h.

question.text: A speed of 72 km/h expressed in metres per second is:

question.text: A speed of 15 metres per second expressed in kilometres per hour is:

question.text: The distance covered in 2 hours and 20 minutes at a speed of 45 km/h is:

question.text: The time taken to cover 360 km at a uniform speed of 80 km/h is:
question.explanation: Time = 360/80 = 4.5 hours.

question.text: A man travels from A to B at 60 km/h and returns at 40 km/h. His average speed for the whole journey is:
question.explanation: Average speed = 2ab/(a+b) = 2 x 60 x 40/100 = 48 km/h.

question.text: Two trains 150 metres and 100 metres long run in opposite directions at 60 km/h and 40 km/h. The time they take to cross each other is:
question.explanation: Relative speed = 100 km/h = 250/9 m/s and the combined length is 250 m, so the time = 250 x 9/250 = 9 seconds.

question.text: A man covers a distance in 3 hours walking at 5 km/h. To cover the same distance in 2 hours and 30 minutes he must walk at:
question.explanation: The distance is 15 km, so the required speed = 15/2.5 = 6 km/h.

question.text: A boat whose speed in still water is 10 km/h travels 36 km downstream in a stream flowing at 2 km/h. The time taken is:
question.explanation: Downstream speed = 10 + 2 = 12 km/h, so the time = 36/12 = 3 hours.

question.text: A train running at 54 km/h crosses a bridge 300 metres long in 30 seconds. The length of the train is:
question.explanation: At 15 m/s the train covers 450 m in 30 seconds, so its length = 450 - 300 = 150 m.

question.text: Two cars start together from the same point in the same direction at 50 km/h and 40 km/h. After 3 hours the distance between them is:
question.explanation: They separate at 10 km/h, so after 3 hours the gap is 30 km.

question.text: A cyclist covers 20 km in 50 minutes. His speed is:
question.explanation: 50 minutes = 5/6 hour, so the speed = 20 x 6/5 = 24 km/h.

question.text: A invests Rs 5,000 and B invests Rs 7,000 in a business for the same period. Out of a profit of Rs 6,000, B's share is:
question.explanation: Profits are shared in the ratio 5 : 7, so B receives 6,000 x 7/12 = Rs 3,500.

question.text: A and B invest Rs 8,000 and Rs 12,000 respectively for the same period. Out of a total profit of Rs 5,000, A receives:
question.explanation: The capital ratio is 2 : 3, so A receives 5,000 x 2/5 = Rs 2,000.

question.text: A invests Rs 3,000 for 12 months and B invests Rs 4,000 for 6 months. Out of a profit of Rs 10,000, A's share is:
question.explanation: Capital-months are 36,000 and 24,000, a ratio of 3 : 2, so A gets 10,000 x 3/5 = Rs 6,000.

question.text: Three partners invest Rs 4,000, Rs 6,000 and Rs 10,000 for the same period. Out of a profit of Rs 10,000 the third partner receives:
question.explanation: The ratio is 2 : 3 : 5, so the third partner receives 10,000 x 5/10 = Rs 5,000.

question.text: A and B share profits in the ratio 3 : 5. If B's share exceeds A's by Rs 800, the total profit is:
question.explanation: The difference is 2 parts = Rs 800, so one part = Rs 400 and the total of 8 parts = Rs 3,200.

question.text: Two partners invest capitals in the ratio 2 : 3 for periods in the ratio 3 : 2. Their profits will be shared in the ratio:
question.explanation: Profit shares follow capital x time = 6 : 6, which reduces to 1 : 1.

question.text: A 40-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 3 : 1. The quantity of milk in it is:
question.explanation: Milk = 40 x 3/4 = 30 litres.

question.text: A 60-litre mixture contains milk and water in the ratio 2 : 1. The water that must be added to make the ratio 1 : 1 is:
question.explanation: The mixture has 40 litres of milk and 20 litres of water, so 20 more litres of water make both equal.

question.text: Rice costing Rs 40 per kg is mixed with rice costing Rs 60 per kg in the ratio 3 : 2. The cost of the mixture per kg is:

question.text: Twenty litres of a milk solution contains 10% water. The quantity of water in it is:
question.explanation: Water = 10% of 20 = 2 litres.

question.text: Fifty litres of a mixture contains 20% alcohol. After adding 10 litres of water the percentage of alcohol becomes:
question.explanation: The alcohol stays at 10 litres while the total becomes 60 litres, so the strength is 10/60 x 100 = 16.67%.

question.text: The value of 3/4 + 2/5 is:
The greatest of the fractions 2/3, 3/5, 5/8 and 7/12 is:

The value of 5/6 - 3/8 is:

question.text: All poets are dreamers. All dreamers are optimists. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: Two universal affirmative premises linked by the middle term 'dreamers' yield the universal conclusion that every poet is an optimist.

question.text: No reptiles are mammals. All cobras are reptiles. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: Cobras fall entirely within the class of reptiles, and that class is wholly excluded from mammals, so no cobra can be a mammal.

question.text: Some students are athletes. All athletes are disciplined. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: The students who are athletes must share every property of athletes, so at least some students are disciplined; nothing is proved about the rest.

question.text: All squares are rectangles. Some rectangles are red. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: A particular affirmative statement can be converted, so 'some rectangles are red' gives 'some red things are rectangles'; the premises never link squares to colour.

question.text: All doctors are graduates. No graduate is illiterate. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: Doctors are contained in the class of graduates, and that class is entirely excluded from the illiterate, so no doctor is illiterate.

question.text: From the statement 'Some books are novels', which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: A particular affirmative proposition converts simply: if some books are novels then some novels are books.

question.text: From the statement 'No politician is honest', which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: No honest person is a politician
question.explanation: A universal negative proposition converts simply, so exclusion between the two classes holds in both directions.

question.text: Given 'All mangoes are fruits', which statement does NOT follow?
options: Whatever is not a fruit is not a mango
question.explanation: Reversing a universal affirmative is invalid; the other three are restatements or the contrapositive of the original.

question.text: All A are B. All B are C. All C are D. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: Class inclusion is transitive, so A is contained in B, B in C and C in D, placing every A inside D.

question.text: No red object is cheap. Some pens are red. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: The pens that are red belong to a class wholly excluded from cheap things, so at least those pens are not cheap.

question.text: All metals conduct electricity. Copper is a metal. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: An individual belonging to a class inherits every property asserted of the whole class.

question.text: Only members may enter the club. Bilal entered the club. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: 'Only members may enter' makes membership a necessary condition of entry, so anyone who entered must be a member.

question.text: Everyone who passes the test receives a certificate. Ahmed did not receive a certificate. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Ahmed did not sit the test
Ahmed did not pass the test
question.explanation: This is modus tollens: denying the consequent of a conditional lets us deny its antecedent.

question.text: In a categorical syllogism, the term that appears in both premises but not in the conclusion is called the
question.explanation: The middle term links the two premises and is dropped from the conclusion; the major and minor terms are the predicate and subject of the conclusion.

question.text: The argument 'All dogs are animals; all cats are animals; therefore all dogs are cats' commits the fallacy of
question.explanation: The middle term 'animals' is not distributed in either premise, so the two classes are never actually connected.

question.text: An argument is valid when
options: the conclusion must be true if the premises are true
its conclusion happens to be true
its premises happen to be true
question.explanation: Validity is about the form of the inference: true premises cannot lead to a false conclusion in a valid argument.

question.text: A sound argument is one that
options: is valid and has all true premises
has a true conclusion but false premises
question.explanation: Soundness adds factual truth of the premises to formal validity.

question.text: All soldiers are brave. Some brave persons are poets. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: Only the second premise can be converted; nothing connects soldiers with poets because the middle term is undistributed.

question.text: No teacher is lazy. All lazy persons are unpunctual. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: No lazy person is a teacher
question.explanation: The first premise converts simply; the premises do not exclude teachers from the wider class of unpunctual persons.

question.text: All P are Q. No Q are R. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: Everything in P lies inside Q, and Q is wholly excluded from R, so P and R cannot overlap.

question.text: Some officers are engineers. All engineers are graduates. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: The officers who are engineers must also be graduates, which establishes a particular, not a universal, conclusion.

question.text: The proverb 'All that glitters is not gold' is logically intended to mean
options: Some things that glitter are not gold
question.explanation: The intended sense is the denial of a universal claim, which is a particular negative: not everything glittering is gold.

question.text: Which statement is logically equivalent to 'If it rains, the match is cancelled'?
options: If it does not rain, the match is not cancelled
The match is cancelled only if it rains
If the match is not cancelled, it did not rain
If the match is cancelled, it rained
question.explanation: A conditional is equivalent only to its contrapositive, formed by negating and interchanging antecedent and consequent.

question.text: The contrapositive of 'If a number is divisible by 4, then it is even' is
options: If a number is even, then it is divisible by 4
If a number is not divisible by 4, then it is not even
If a number is odd, then it is divisible by 4
If a number is not even, then it is not divisible by 4
question.explanation: The contrapositive negates both parts and reverses their order, and it always has the same truth value as the original.

question.text: The converse of 'If x is a bird, then x has feathers' is
options: If x has feathers, then x is a bird
If x is not a bird, then x has no feathers
If x has no feathers, then x is not a bird
x is a bird and x has feathers
question.explanation: The converse simply interchanges antecedent and consequent, and it does not follow from the original statement.

question.text: If a metal is heated it expands. This metal did not expand. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: The metal is not really a metal
question.explanation: Denying the consequent of a true conditional validly denies its antecedent (modus tollens).

question.text: 'If a student cheats he is disqualified. Aslam was disqualified, therefore Aslam cheated.' This reasoning commits the fallacy of
question.explanation: Disqualification may have other causes; inferring the antecedent from the consequent is invalid.

question.text: 'If it snows the road is closed. It did not snow, therefore the road is not closed.' This reasoning commits the fallacy of
question.explanation: The conditional says nothing about what happens when it does not snow, so the road may still be closed for another reason.

question.text: Either the fuse is blown or the bulb is dead. The fuse is not blown. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: The bulb is in working order
question.explanation: In a disjunctive syllogism, denying one alternative of a true disjunction establishes the other.

question.text: If P then Q, and if Q then R. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: If not P then not R
question.explanation: Conditionals chain together in a hypothetical syllogism, giving the transitive conditional from P to R.

question.text: 'Only if you submit the form will you be registered.' This statement means that submitting the form is
question.explanation: 'Only if' introduces a necessary condition; it does not promise that submission alone guarantees registration.

question.text: Passing the written test is a necessary but not sufficient condition for appointment. It follows that
options: nobody who fails the test is appointed
everyone who passes the test is appointed
only those who fail the test are appointed
the test has no bearing on appointment
question.explanation: A necessary condition must be met by every appointee, but meeting it does not by itself secure appointment.

question.text: The correct denial of the statement 'All students passed' is
options: At least one student did not pass
question.explanation: The contradictory of a universal affirmative is a particular negative, requiring only one exception.

question.text: The correct denial of the statement 'Some birds can swim' is
question.explanation: The contradictory of a particular affirmative is the universal negative covering every member of the class.

question.text: The expression 'if and only if' states
options: both a necessary and a sufficient condition
question.explanation: A biconditional asserts that each side implies the other, so the condition is both necessary and sufficient.

question.text: 'No pass, no entry' is logically equivalent to
options: A pass may be shown after entry
If a person enters, that person has a pass
If a person has a pass, that person enters
question.explanation: 'If no pass then no entry' is a conditional whose contrapositive is 'if entry then a pass'.

question.text: A conditional statement and its contrapositive are
options: equivalent only when both are false
question.explanation: Negating and interchanging the two parts preserves truth value in every case.

question.text: Either the report is wrong or the machine is faulty. The machine is not faulty. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: The machine must still be replaced
Both the report and the machine are in order
question.explanation: Eliminating one disjunct of a true disjunction leaves the other one standing.

question.text: A is taller than B. C is shorter than B. Who is the tallest of the three?
options: B and C are of equal height
question.explanation: A stands above B and B stands above C, so A occupies the top of the order.

question.text: P is heavier than Q, Q is heavier than R, and R is heavier than S. Who is the lightest?
question.explanation: The chain of comparisons runs P, Q, R, S from heaviest to lightest.

question.text: X is older than Y and Y is older than Z. Which statement must be true?
question.explanation: The 'older than' relation is transitive, so the order runs X, Y, Z from oldest to youngest.

question.text: In a race Ali finished ahead of Bilal, Bilal finished ahead of Danish, and Danish finished ahead of Ehsan. Who finished last?
question.explanation: The stated order is Ali, Bilal, Danish, Ehsan, so Ehsan is at the end of it.

question.text: Amina scored more than Bushra, and Chanda scored less than Bushra. Which statement must be true?
options: Bushra scored the highest of the three
question.explanation: Amina is above Bushra and Bushra is above Chanda, so Amina must be above Chanda.

question.text: All members of the committee are lawyers. Sana is not a lawyer. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Sana is not a member of the committee
Sana is a member of the committee
Some lawyers are not committee members
question.explanation: Anyone outside the class of lawyers must lie outside the committee, which is contained in that class.

question.text: Every book on the shelf is in Urdu. This dictionary is in English. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: This dictionary is not on the shelf
This dictionary is on the shelf
question.explanation: An item lacking the property common to everything on the shelf cannot be on the shelf.

question.text: No student in the class is above 20 years of age. Kamran is 22 years old. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Kamran is not a student anywhere
Some students in the class are 22
Kamran is not in the class
question.explanation: Kamran fails the age condition satisfied by every member of the class, so he cannot be a member.

question.text: All the pens in the box are blue. This pen is red. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: This pen did not come from the box
This pen came from the box
The box contains some red pens
question.explanation: Since every pen in the box is blue, a red pen must have some other source.

question.text: Aslam is sitting between Bashir and Chand, and Bashir is to Aslam's left. Which statement must be true?
options: Aslam is at one end of the row
question.explanation: Aslam has one neighbour on each side; with Bashir on the left, Chand must be on the right.

question.text: Five persons stand in a row. Q is exactly in the middle and P stands immediately to Q's left. How many persons stand to the left of P?
question.explanation: Q occupies the third place and P the second, so exactly one person stands to P's left.

question.text: Whenever it rains the road becomes wet. The road is dry today. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
options: Rain does not affect the road
question.explanation: If rain always produced a wet road, a dry road rules out rain (modus tollens).

question.text: All A are B. No B is C. Some C are D. Which conclusion must be true?
question.explanation: A lies wholly inside B and B is wholly outside C, so A and C cannot overlap; nothing follows about D.

question.text: A man says, 'All my sons are engineers.' Rashid is his son. Which conclusion necessarily follows?
question.explanation: A property asserted of every member of a group applies to any named member of it.

question.text: 'Do not accept his economic plan; he failed in his own business years ago.' This argument commits the fallacy of
question.explanation: The reasoning attacks the person's record instead of examining the merits of the plan itself.

question.text: 'My opponent wants to reduce the defence budget, so clearly he wants the country left defenceless.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: The opponent's position is exaggerated into an absurd version that is easier to attack.

question.text: 'Nobody has ever proved that ghosts do not exist, so ghosts must exist.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: Absence of disproof is treated as proof, which the argumentum ad ignorantiam wrongly allows.

question.text: 'Millions of people buy this brand, so it must be the best.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: Widespread acceptance is not evidence of quality; the argumentum ad populum substitutes numbers for reasons.

question.text: 'Please raise my grade, sir; my family will be heartbroken if I fail.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: Sympathy is offered in place of any evidence that the grade was wrongly awarded.

question.text: 'Approve my proposal, or remember that your contract comes up for renewal next month.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: A veiled threat, not evidence, is used to secure agreement (argumentum ad baculum).

question.text: 'Either we abolish every subsidy or the economy will collapse.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: Only two extreme options are presented although many intermediate possibilities exist.

question.text: 'If students are allowed to retake one paper, they will soon demand to retake every paper and the examination system will collapse.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: A chain of increasingly serious consequences is asserted without any evidence that the first step leads to the last.

question.text: 'This law is just because it is right, and it is right because it is just.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: The conclusion is used as its own support, so the argument moves in a closed circle.

question.text: 'I wore my lucky shirt and the team won, so the shirt brought the victory.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: Mere sequence in time is mistaken for a causal connection.

question.text: 'I met two rude people from that city, so everyone there is rude.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: A sweeping conclusion is drawn from a sample far too small to support it.

question.text: 'Every player in the side is outstanding, so the side as a whole must be outstanding.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: Properties of the individual parts are transferred without warrant to the whole.

question.text: 'That is a very wealthy company, so every one of its employees must be wealthy.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: A property of the whole is wrongly assigned to each of its parts.

question.text: 'A feather is light; what is light cannot be dark; therefore a feather cannot be dark.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: The word 'light' shifts from meaning low in weight to meaning pale in colour within the same argument.

question.text: Asked about rising inflation, a speaker replies with a long description of the beauty of the northern areas. This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: An irrelevant subject is introduced to draw attention away from the question asked.

question.text: 'You advise me to give up smoking, but you smoke yourself, so your advice is worthless.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: The adviser's own conduct is irrelevant to whether the advice is correct; this is the 'you too' form of ad hominem.

question.text: 'A famous cricketer says this syrup cures diabetes, so it must cure diabetes.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: The person cited is respected in a field unrelated to medicine, so his endorsement is not evidence.

question.text: 'Running a country is exactly like running a household, so a government should never borrow money.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: The two cases differ in essential respects, so the comparison cannot carry the conclusion.

question.text: 'This practice must be wrong because it began during the colonial period.' This is the fallacy of
question.explanation: The argument judges an idea by its origin rather than by its present merits.

question.text: The fallacy of assuming that what is true of a whole must be true of each of its parts is called
question.explanation: Division moves from whole to parts; composition moves in the opposite direction, from parts to whole.

question.text: The fallacy of using the same word in two different senses within one argument is called
question.explanation: Equivocation trades on an ambiguity of a single term; amphiboly arises from ambiguous grammar instead.

question.text: The fallacy in which the conclusion is already assumed in the premises is known as
question.explanation: Petitio principii offers as support the very claim that is supposed to be proved.

question.text: The Latin phrase 'post hoc ergo propter hoc' means
options: after this, therefore because of this
question.explanation: It names the error of treating a later event as caused by an earlier one merely because it followed.

question.text: 'Argumentum ad hominem' literally means an argument directed
question.explanation: The attack is aimed at the person advancing the claim rather than at the claim itself.

question.text: 'Argumentum ad populum' is an appeal to
options: the beliefs or feelings of the crowd
question.explanation: It urges acceptance of a claim because many people already accept it.

question.text: 'Argumentum ad baculum' is an appeal to
question.explanation: 'Baculum' means a stick, so the phrase names the appeal to coercion rather than to evidence.

question.text: Statement: 'Take our tablet and your headache will disappear within ten minutes.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: People want quick relief from headache
Every tablet acts within ten minutes
Headache cannot be relieved in any other way
Our tablet is the cheapest available
question.explanation: The appeal only works if speed of relief is something the reader values; the other statements go far beyond what is taken for granted.

question.text: Statement: 'Boil the water before drinking it.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Boiling improves the taste of water
All diseases are spread through water
Unboiled water may be unsafe to drink
question.explanation: The advice makes sense only if the water as supplied carries some risk that boiling removes.

question.text: Statement: 'The examination centre has been shifted to the college because more candidates applied this year.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: The old centre has been demolished
Candidates prefer colleges to other buildings
Examinations must always be held in colleges
The college can seat more candidates than the old centre
question.explanation: The stated reason works only if the new venue solves the problem of extra candidates, that is, it has greater capacity.

question.text: Statement: 'Submit the form before 5 p.m.; forms received later will not be accepted.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Applicants are able to submit the form before 5 p.m.
No applicant will submit the form at all
The office remains closed during the day
question.explanation: Setting a deadline presupposes that those addressed are in a position to meet it.

question.text: Statement: 'In case of fire use the stairs; do not use the lift.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Stairs are always wider than lifts
Fires break out only in tall buildings
Lifts are more expensive to run
The lift may become unsafe during a fire
question.explanation: The instruction rests on the belief that the lift carries a risk in a fire that the stairs do not.

question.text: Statement: 'Write your roll number on the answer sheet.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Every candidate has been given a roll number
question.explanation: The instruction can be obeyed only if each candidate actually possesses a roll number.

question.text: Statement: 'The company has announced a bonus for workers in order to raise production.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Production cannot be raised by any other means
question.explanation: The measure presupposes a link between extra pay and extra output; the other options are not needed for the plan to make sense.

question.text: Statement: 'Read the instructions on the packet before using this medicine.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: The medicine is dangerous in every dose
All users are trained in medicine
The instructions are printed in Urdu
question.explanation: The direction assumes the existence of instructions on the packet; nothing else is required for it to be sensible.

question.text: Statement: 'Because of the fuel shortage the government has advised offices to work four days a week.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: The shortage will last for ever
Working fewer days will reduce fuel consumption
question.explanation: The advice is a means to an end and presupposes that the shorter week actually saves fuel.

question.text: Statement: 'Buy a helmet and ride safely.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Wearing a helmet makes riding safer
Riding without a helmet is impossible
question.explanation: The advertisement links the purchase to safety, which presupposes that the helmet contributes to it.

question.text: In the analysis of an argument, an assumption is
options: a definition of the terms used
something taken for granted but not stated
question.explanation: An assumption is an unstated premise that the argument needs in order to work.

question.text: Statement: 'Notice: all employees must attend the training session on Monday.' Which assumption is implicit in this statement?
options: Employees will be available on Monday
Employees know nothing about their work
question.explanation: A compulsory session presupposes that those required to attend can in fact be present that day.

question.text: Event A: the price of petrol was raised on Monday. Event B: taxi fares were increased on Tuesday. Which relation is most reasonable?
options: A is the cause and B is the effect
B is the cause and A is the effect
The two events are entirely unconnected
Both are effects of a fall in demand
question.explanation: Fuel is a direct input cost for taxis, and the increase in fares followed the rise in price.

question.text: Ice-cream sales and cases of heat stroke both rise sharply in June. The best explanation is that
options: heat stroke causes people to buy ice-cream
the two figures are recorded wrongly
both are effects of the hot weather
question.explanation: A third factor, high temperature, produces both trends, so the correlation between them is not causal.

question.text: The reasoning 'cities with more police also record more crime, therefore police cause crime' overlooks the principle that
options: correlation does not by itself establish causation
question.explanation: Two things may vary together because one drives the other in the reverse direction or because a third factor drives both.

question.text: A survey shows that students who sleep longer obtain higher marks. Which finding would most weaken the claim that extra sleep causes higher marks?
options: Sleep is necessary for good health
Well-organised students both sleep longer and study more effectively
question.explanation: It supplies a common third factor that could produce both the longer sleep and the better marks.

question.text: In a controlled experiment the purpose of the control group is
options: to reduce the cost of the experiment
to confirm what the researcher expects
to provide a comparison in which the suspected cause is absent
to increase the total number of participants
question.explanation: Only by comparing with a group not exposed to the factor can a change be attributed to that factor.

question.text: Event A: heavy rain fell throughout the night. Event B: the low-lying road was under water in the morning. Which relation is most reasonable?
options: B is the cause and A is the effect
Both are effects of an unrelated cause
There is no connection between them
A is the cause and B is the effect
question.explanation: The rain preceded the flooding and is sufficient to explain water collecting on low ground.

question.text: Which of the following is a necessary condition for ordinary combustion?
question.explanation: Ordinary burning cannot occur without an oxidising agent, whereas the particular fuel or the weather may vary.

question.text: 'Since the new mayor took office, road accidents have fallen.' Before crediting the mayor, one must first rule out
options: the geographical size of the city
the cost of building the roads
other changes such as new traffic rules or fewer vehicles on the road
question.explanation: A causal claim survives only when alternative explanations for the same change have been eliminated.

question.text: Question: should smoking be prohibited in enclosed public places? Which is the strongest argument?
options: No, because some people enjoy it
Yes, because the smoke inhaled by others damages their health
No, because smokers also pay taxes
question.explanation: An argument is strong when it is relevant and rests on a substantial consequence, here harm to non-smokers.

question.text: Question: should public transport fares be subsidised? Which of the following arguments is weak?
options: No, because the transport minister is personally unpopular
Yes, because low fares help low-income commuters
No, because subsidies enlarge the fiscal deficit
Yes, because cheaper transport reduces the use of private cars
question.explanation: An argument that turns on a person rather than on the policy is irrelevant and therefore weak.

question.text: A strong argument is one that is
options: held by a large number of people
relevant to the issue and supported by evidence
question.explanation: Strength depends on relevance and evidential support, not on length, popularity or the speaker's fame.

question.text: Which of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument that wearing seat belts should be compulsory?
options: Seat belts are made of strong woven fabric
Most new cars are fitted with seat belts
Several other countries have such a law
Seat belts sharply reduce deaths in road accidents
question.explanation: Direct evidence that the measure saves lives supports the case, while the other statements are merely incidental.

question.text: Which of the following, if true, most weakens the claim that a town's new filtration plant has made its water safe?
options: The plant was inaugurated by a senior official
A few residents continue to buy bottled water
Tests taken after installation still show bacteria above the permitted limit
The plant cost more than was estimated
question.explanation: Test results bearing directly on water quality contradict the claim; cost, ceremony and habit do not.

question.text: An argument that offers only emotional appeal and no supporting evidence is best described as
question.explanation: Without relevant evidence an argument fails to support its conclusion, however moving it may be.

question.text: In evaluating arguments, 'relevance' means that the argument
options: is short and easy to read
bears directly on the question under discussion
question.explanation: A relevant argument addresses the actual issue; irrelevant material cannot support the conclusion however true it is.

question.text: Statement: cracks have appeared in a bridge carrying heavy traffic on a national highway. Which course of action is most appropriate?
options: Wait until the cracks widen further
Ban all vehicles throughout the province
Close the bridge to traffic and have it inspected at once
Raise the toll charged on the bridge
question.explanation: The immediate danger to life requires the traffic to be stopped and the structure examined; the other steps are irrelevant or excessive.

question.text: Statement: an outbreak of dengue fever has been reported in a city. Which course of action is most appropriate?
options: Close all schools in the country permanently
Prohibit the sale of mosquito nets
Shift the population of the city elsewhere
Remove stagnant water and spray the affected localities
question.explanation: Dengue spreads through mosquitoes that breed in standing water, so removing breeding sites attacks the cause.

question.text: Statement: an unusually large number of candidates failed a departmental examination this year. Which course of action is most appropriate?
options: Examine the reasons for the poor result and arrange remedial training
question.explanation: Finding the cause before acting is the reasonable step; the other options either avoid the problem or punish without evidence.

question.text: Statement: a public office receives repeated complaints about long queues at its counters. Which course of action is most appropriate?
options: Reduce the working hours of the office
Close half of the existing counters
Introduce an appointment and token system and open more counters at peak hours
question.explanation: Managing the flow of visitors addresses the cause of the queues, while the other measures would worsen the situation.

question.text: Statement: a school reports that many pupils arrive without breakfast and lose attention in class. Which course of action is most appropriate?
options: Start a school meal scheme and inform parents of the problem
Expel the pupils who lose attention
question.explanation: Providing food and involving parents removes the stated cause of inattention; the other steps punish the pupils instead.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Punjab, Lahore, Karachi, Peshawar?
question.explanation: Karachi, Lahore and Peshawar are cities, while Punjab is a province.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Iron, Copper, Bronze, Aluminium?
question.explanation: Copper, iron and aluminium are pure metallic elements; bronze is an alloy of copper and tin.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Rose, Mango, Lily, Jasmine?
question.explanation: Rose, lily and jasmine are flowers; mango is a fruit.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Eye, Ear, Nose, Lung?
question.explanation: Eye, ear and nose are sense organs; the lung is a respiratory organ.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Sparrow, Emu, Ostrich, Kiwi?
question.explanation: Ostrich, emu and kiwi are flightless birds; the sparrow can fly.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Square, Rectangle, Triangle, Rhombus?
question.explanation: Square, rectangle and rhombus have four sides; the triangle has three.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Litre, Metre, Gallon, Pint?
question.explanation: Litre, gallon and pint measure volume; the metre measures length.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Indus, Jhelum, Chenab, Karakoram?
question.explanation: Indus, Jhelum and Chenab are rivers; Karakoram is a mountain range.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Cotton, Wheat, Rice, Maize?
question.explanation: Wheat, rice and maize are food grains; cotton is a fibre crop.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: April, June, August, September?
question.explanation: April, June and September have 30 days each; August has 31.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Mercury, Moon, Venus, Mars?
question.explanation: Mercury, Venus and Mars are planets; the Moon is a natural satellite.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Hammer, Screwdriver, Saw, Nail?
question.explanation: Hammer, saw and screwdriver are tools; a nail is a fastener worked on by tools.

question.text: Which one does not belong to the group: Sahara, Amazon, Nile, Danube?
question.explanation: Nile, Amazon and Danube are rivers; the Sahara is a desert.

question.text: Which number does not belong to the group: 3, 5, 9, 7?
question.explanation: 3, 5 and 7 are prime numbers, while 9 is composite (3 x 3).

question.text: Which number does not belong to the group: 8, 100, 27, 64?
question.explanation: 8, 27 and 64 are perfect cubes of 2, 3 and 4; 100 is not a perfect cube.

question.text: Which number does not belong to the group: 49, 64, 81, 80?
question.explanation: 49, 64 and 81 are the squares of 7, 8 and 9; 80 is not a perfect square.

question.text: Which number does not belong to the group: 21, 17, 13, 19?
question.explanation: 13, 17 and 19 are prime; 21 is divisible by 3 and 7.

question.text: Which number does not belong to the group: 15, 25, 42, 35?
question.explanation: 15, 25 and 35 are multiples of 5; 42 is not.

question.text: Which number does not belong to the group: 4, 20, 16, 8?
question.explanation: 4, 8 and 16 are powers of 2; 20 is not.

question.text: Which number does not belong to the group: 121, 144, 169, 180?
question.explanation: 121, 144 and 169 are the squares of 11, 12 and 13; 180 is not a perfect square.

question.text: Doctor is to Patient as Lawyer is to:
question.explanation: A doctor renders professional service to a patient just as a lawyer does to a client.

question.text: Pen is to Write as Knife is to:
question.explanation: The pair links an instrument with its function: a pen is used to write, a knife to cut.

question.text: Bird is to Nest as Bee is to:
question.explanation: The relation is creature to its dwelling: a bird lives in a nest, a bee in a hive.

question.text: Foot is to Shoe as Hand is to:
question.explanation: A shoe is the covering worn on the foot, as a glove is the covering worn on the hand.

question.text: Cat is to Kitten as Dog is to:
question.explanation: The relation is adult to young: a young cat is a kitten and a young dog is a puppy.

question.text: Teacher is to School as Judge is to:
question.explanation: The relation is professional to workplace: a teacher works in a school, a judge in a court.

question.text: Thermometer is to Temperature as Barometer is to:
question.explanation: Each instrument is paired with what it measures; a barometer measures atmospheric pressure.

question.text: Island is to Water as Oasis is to:
question.explanation: An island is land surrounded by water, and an oasis is a fertile patch surrounded by desert.

question.text: Sculptor is to Statue as Poet is to:
question.explanation: The relation is maker to the work produced: a sculptor makes a statue, a poet composes a poem.

question.text: Circle is to Sphere as Square is to:
question.explanation: A sphere is the three-dimensional counterpart of a circle, and a cube is that of a square.

question.text: Carpenter is to Wood as Blacksmith is to:
question.explanation: The relation is craftsman to the material worked upon: a carpenter works with wood, a blacksmith with iron.

question.text: Ship is to Captain as Aeroplane is to:
question.explanation: The relation is vehicle to the person who commands it; an aeroplane is flown by a pilot.

question.text: Frog is to Amphibian as Snake is to:
question.explanation: The relation is animal to its class; the snake belongs to the class of reptiles.

question.text: Deaf is to Hearing as Blind is to:
question.explanation: A deaf person lacks hearing, and a blind person lacks sight.

question.text: Pakistan is to Islamabad as Turkey is to:
question.explanation: The relation is country to capital; Ankara, not Istanbul, is the capital of Turkey.

question.text: Wheat is to Flour as Sugarcane is to:
question.explanation: The relation is raw crop to the product processed from it; sugarcane yields sugar.

question.text: Novel is to Chapter as Poem is to:
question.explanation: A chapter is a division of a novel, as a stanza is a division of a poem.

question.text: Zoology is to Animals as Botany is to:
question.explanation: Each branch of science is paired with its subject matter; botany is the study of plants.

question.text: Ornithology is to Birds as Entomology is to:
question.explanation: Ornithology is the study of birds and entomology is the study of insects.

question.text: Melting is to Liquid as Freezing is to:
question.explanation: Melting produces a liquid, while freezing produces a solid.

question.text: If 3 : 10 and 5 : 26, then 7 : ?
question.explanation: Each second term is the square of the first plus 1, so 7 gives 49 + 1 = 50.

question.text: If 2 : 5 and 4 : 9, then 6 : ?
question.explanation: Each second term is twice the first plus 1, so 6 gives 12 + 1 = 13.

question.text: If 3 : 12 and 5 : 30, then 7 : ?
question.explanation: Each second term is the first multiplied by the next integer, so 7 gives 7 x 8 = 56.

question.text: If 2 : 7 and 3 : 13, then 4 : ?
question.explanation: The rule is n squared plus n plus 1, so 4 gives 16 + 4 + 1 = 21.

question.text: If 5 : 24 and 7 : 48, then 9 : ?
question.explanation: Each second term is the square of the first minus 1, so 9 gives 81 - 1 = 80.

question.text: If 2 : 8 and 3 : 27, then 4 : ?
question.explanation: Each second term is the cube of the first, so 4 gives 4 x 4 x 4 = 64.

question.text: If 6 : 18 and 8 : 32, then 10 : ?
question.explanation: Each second term is half the square of the first, so 10 gives 100 / 2 = 50.

question.text: If 9 : 3 and 25 : 5, then 64 : ?
question.explanation: Each second term is the square root of the first, and the square root of 64 is 8.

question.text: If 12 : 4 and 21 : 7, then 27 : ?
question.explanation: Each second term is one third of the first, so 27 gives 27 / 3 = 9.
Each second term is the square of the first, so 13 gives 13 x 13 = 169.

question.text: If 4 : 13 and 6 : 19, then 9 : ?
question.explanation: Each second term is three times the first plus 1, so 9 gives 27 + 1 = 28.

question.text: If 1 : 4 and 2 : 9, then 4 : ?
question.explanation: Each second term is the square of one more than the first, so 4 gives 5 x 5 = 25.

question.text: Aeroplane, helicopter and glider form one class. Which of the following belongs to the same class?
question.explanation: All the given items are means of air transport, and a hot-air balloon also travels through the air.

question.text: Copper, zinc and nickel form one class. Which of the following belongs to the same class?
question.explanation: The three named substances are pure metallic elements, and cobalt is also an element, whereas bronze, brass and steel are alloys.

question.text: Triangle, quadrilateral and pentagon form one class. Which of the following belongs to the same class?
question.explanation: All three are polygons bounded by straight sides, and a hexagon is a six-sided polygon.

question.text: Sparrow, crow and pigeon form one class. Which of the following belongs to the same class?
question.explanation: The three named creatures are birds, and the parrot is also a bird, while a bat and a squirrel are mammals and a butterfly is an insect.

question.text: Rupee, dollar and dinar form one class. Which of the following belongs to the same class?
question.explanation: All three are currencies, and the riyal is likewise a currency.

question.text: Kidney, liver and heart form one class. Which of the following belongs to the same class?
question.explanation: The three named items are internal organs of the body, and the lung is also an organ.

question.text: Mango, banana and apple form one class. Which of the following belongs to the same class?
question.explanation: The three named items are fruits, and guava is also a fruit while the others are vegetables.

question.text: Hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen form one class. Which of the following belongs to the same class?
question.explanation: The three named gases are chemical elements, and helium is also an element, whereas the other options are compounds.

question.text: Square, rhombus and rectangle form one class. Which of the following belongs to the same class?
question.explanation: All three are four-sided figures, and a trapezium is also a quadrilateral.

question.text: Poetry, drama and novel form one class. Which of the following belongs to the same class?
question.explanation: The three named items are forms of literature, and the essay is also a literary form.

question.text: Which pair of unit and quantity is correctly matched?
question.explanation: The watt is the SI unit of power; the newton measures force, the joule energy and the pascal pressure.

question.text: Which pair of scientist and discovery is correctly matched?
question.explanation: Alexander Fleming discovered penicillin in 1928; the other three pairings are false.

question.text: Which pair of country and currency is correctly matched?
question.explanation: The currency of Japan is the yen; China uses the yuan, Bangladesh the taka and Iran the rial.

question.text: Which pair of animal and dwelling is correctly matched?
question.explanation: A horse is kept in a stable; a lion lives in a den, a bee in a hive and a sparrow in a nest.

question.text: Which pair of instrument and use is correctly matched?
question.explanation: A hygrometer measures humidity; a seismograph records earthquakes, a lactometer checks the purity of milk and a barometer measures atmospheric pressure.

question.text: Which pair of collective noun and group is correctly matched?
question.explanation: Bees move in a swarm; cattle form a herd, birds a flock and fish a shoal.

question.text: Which pair of province and its capital is correctly matched?
question.explanation: Quetta is the provincial capital of Balochistan; the capitals of Sindh, Punjab and Khyber Pakhtunkhwa are Karachi, Lahore and Peshawar.

question.text: Which pair of book and author is correctly matched?
question.explanation: Bang-e-Dara is the Urdu poetry collection of Allama Iqbal; Gulistan is by Saadi, Shahnama by Firdausi and Masnavi by Rumi.

question.text: Which pair shows the same relationship as Cow : Calf?
question.explanation: The relationship is adult animal to its young; the young of a horse is a foal.

question.text: Which pair shows the same relationship as Doctor : Stethoscope?
question.explanation: The relationship is worker to the tool he uses; a farmer uses a plough, while the other options name places.

question.text: Which pair shows the same relationship as Kilogram : Mass?
question.explanation: The relationship is unit to the quantity it measures; the ampere measures electric current.

question.text: Which pair shows the same relationship as Hot : Cold?
question.explanation: Hot and cold are opposites, and only ancient and modern are opposites; the other pairs are synonyms.

question.text: Which pair shows the same relationship as Chapter : Book?
question.explanation: A chapter is a part of a book, and a room is a part of a house; the other pairs place the whole before the part.

question.text: In the table below every row follows the same rule: Row 1 is 4, 5, 20; Row 2 is 6, 3, 18; Row 3 is 7, 8, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The third entry of each row is the product of the first two, so 7 x 8 = 56.

question.text: In the table below every row follows the same rule: Row 1 is 9, 4, 5; Row 2 is 12, 7, 5; Row 3 is 15, 6, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The third entry is the first minus the second, so 15 - 6 = 9.

question.text: In the table below every row follows the same rule: Row 1 is 3, 5, 34; Row 2 is 4, 6, 52; Row 3 is 5, 7, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The third entry is the sum of the squares of the first two, so 25 + 49 = 74.

question.text: In the table below every row follows the same rule: Row 1 is 6, 4, 20; Row 2 is 8, 3, 22; Row 3 is 9, 5, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The third entry is twice the sum of the first two, so 2 x (9 + 5) = 28.

question.text: In the table below every row follows the same rule: Row 1 is 5, 4, 15; Row 2 is 6, 3, 12; Row 3 is 7, 5, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The third entry is the product of the first two minus the first number, so 35 - 7 = 28.

question.text: In the table below every row follows the same rule: Row 1 is 8, 4, 6; Row 2 is 10, 6, 8; Row 3 is 14, 8, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The third entry is the average of the first two, so (14 + 8) / 2 = 11.

question.text: In a 3 by 3 grid every row adds up to the same total: Row 1 is 8, 1, 6; Row 2 is 3, 5, 7; Row 3 is 4, 9, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: Each row totals 15, and 15 - 4 - 9 = 2.

question.text: In the table below every column follows the same rule: Column 1 is 5, 4, 21; Column 2 is 7, 9, 40; Column 3 is 8, 14, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The third entry is the square of the first minus the second, so 64 - 14 = 50.

question.text: In the table below every row follows the same rule: Row 1 is 2, 3, 11; Row 2 is 4, 5, 29; Row 3 is 3, 6, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The third entry is the product of the first two plus their sum, so 18 + 9 = 27.

question.text: In the table below every row follows the same rule: Row 1 is 18, 3, 6; Row 2 is 28, 4, 7; Row 3 is 45, 5, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The third entry is the first divided by the second, so 45 / 5 = 9.

question.text: In the table below every row follows the same rule: Row 1 is 7, 2, 45; Row 2 is 9, 4, 65; Row 3 is 10, 6, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The third entry is the square of the first minus the square of the second, so 100 - 36 = 64.

question.text: In the table below every row follows the same rule: Row 1 is 2, 4, 8; Row 2 is 3, 9, 27; Row 3 is 4, 16, ?. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: Each row gives a number, its square and its cube, so the missing entry is 4 cubed, that is 64.

question.text: In the table below the middle number of each row is the average of the outer two: Row 1 is 4, 7, 10; Row 2 is 6, 11, 16; Row 3 is 9, ?, 21. What number replaces the question mark?
question.explanation: The average of 9 and 21 is (9 + 21) / 2 = 15.

question.text: A table records a shop's sales as Monday 120 units, Tuesday 150 units, Wednesday 90 units and Thursday 160 units. What is the average number of units sold per day?
question.explanation: The total is 520 units over four days, and 520 divided by 4 is 130.

question.text: A student's marks, each out of 100, are Urdu 72, English 65, Mathematics 88 and Science 75. What is his average percentage?
question.explanation: The marks total 300 out of 400, so the average is 300 divided by 4, that is 75 per cent.

question.text: A college enrolment table shows Arts 250 students, Science 400 students and Commerce 150 students. What percentage of the total enrolment is in Science?
question.explanation: The total enrolment is 800, and 400 out of 800 is 50 per cent.

question.text: A monthly budget table shows rent Rs 12,000, food Rs 9,000, transport Rs 3,000 and other items Rs 6,000. What fraction of the total expenditure is spent on food?
question.explanation: The total expenditure is Rs 30,000, and 9,000 out of 30,000 equals 3/10.

question.text: A rainfall table shows January 25 mm, February 40 mm, March 15 mm and April 60 mm. What is the difference between the highest and the lowest monthly rainfall?
question.explanation: The highest is 60 mm in April and the lowest 15 mm in March, and 60 - 15 = 45 mm.

question.text: A table shows that a town's population was 50,000 in 2010 and 65,000 in 2020. What was the percentage increase over the decade?
question.explanation: The rise is 15,000 on a base of 50,000, and 15,000 divided by 50,000 is 30 per cent.

question.text: A table of test marks out of 50 shows Ali 35, Bilal 42, Sara 28 and Hina 45. How many of the four scored more than 60 per cent?
question.explanation: Sixty per cent of 50 is 30 marks, and Ali, Bilal and Hina all scored above 30.

question.text: A production table shows unit A made 240 items and unit B made 180 items. What is the ratio of unit A's output to unit B's output?
question.explanation: The ratio 240 to 180 reduces to 4 : 3 after dividing both numbers by 60.

question.text: A table of daily maximum temperatures gives 30, 34, 28, 36 and 32 degrees Celsius for five days. What is the average daily maximum temperature?
question.explanation: The five readings total 160 degrees, and 160 divided by 5 is 32 degrees.

question.text: A library table shows books issued as Monday 45, Tuesday 60, Wednesday 35, Thursday 50 and Friday 60. On how many days were more than 45 books issued?
